Hansard of tomorrow will show what the hon. member said. Whether the views put forward by Dr. Bush could best be implemented in that way is a matter of opinion. I should like to refer the hon. member to another passage in Dr. Vannevar Bush's book at page 114, where he said:
To spread our entire thinking before a potential enemy is senseless; it gives him a very real advantage, and an avoidable one. There is a reasonable balance between keeping our people informed and intelligent and unnecessarily supplying data to a potential enemy.
Since the war ended we have at times erred and departed from this balance. As new aircraft have been developed, we have described their performance in some detail, published photographs of them, and discussed their merits and limitations. When a new guided missile flies well, the whole world knows of its success. We even discuss parts of our war plans, and examine in the full light of public discussion the relative merits of carriers and land-based planes for strategic bombardment, spreading out concepts of how we would use our power for all to read. Doing these things does not make sense.
Dr. Vannevar Bush is one of the world's great leaders in the field of scientific research. He is certainly one with whom my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and people like Dr. O. M. Solandt were very glad to work when the going was tough. It has been suggested by the hon. and gallant member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) that giving information to a parliamentary committee of the character described would allay fears. I do not think that has been the result of giving that kind of information in the country which has the type of committee that hon. members of the opposition seem to want. I do not think so.
Of course I believe we are in a very difficult period. We must give all possible information, and we must also do everything possible to sustain the confidence of the people. I

believe it was the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) who said that if a committee were established it would help recruiting. Our recruiting for the active forces, the navy, army and air force, does not need any help. We are getting all the men we want. They are first-class men of fine character.

maintopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Unemployment.

maintopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
That is interesting. I should like to take up the hon. member on that statement. I can give him some figures. When I last spoke to the house on the subject of defence on the 11th of November I put before the house the results of recruiting for the twelve months ending the 30th of September, 1949. In the introduction of the defence estimates, which I hope to make on Friday, I will put before the house the results of recruiting for the twelve months ending the 30th of January, 1950, four months later. No doubt the hon. member would suggest that during that period we should have had a great influx of recruits owing to unemployment. Not at all. We have had a slight decline resulting from our increased standards and our diminishing pressure. What is more, we have had just about the same number of applicants in respect of each twelve-month period, indicating that what the hon. gentleman suggests is simply not so.
As to the question of recruiting, because it has some bearing on the discussion, I believe that hon. members must now appreciate, because it has been said time after time, that we can only spend each defence dollar once. We can spend it on construction; we can spend it on equipment; we can spend it on personnel, but we cannot spend the same dollar twice. Therefore the problem of defence planning-and that is what we are concerned with-is finding out on the basis of the best information available what proportion of the amount that parliament and the country are willing to spend on defence should be spent on construction, equipment and personnel. We cannot spend the same money twice.
Then you have the same thing when you come to the allocation between the navy, army, air force, defence research and development. The allocation must be made, and under this government it is made by the cabinet on the advice of the cabinet defence committee, and in respect of matters affecting all three services on the joint advice of the chiefs of staff acting through their committee. When it comes down to a question concerning only one service, then it is done by the chief of staff with my approval, and subject always to the approval of the cabinet defence committee, the treasury board and the government. This planning oneration is continuous.

We plan to meet events that may develop three, four or five years ahead. We plan for steady development, but we also plan so that we will be able to make adjustments as they may be indicated to be necessary by the changing march of events. As to the distribution of our defence dollar, I propose to deal with it at some length on Friday in order to indicate to hon. members and the country at large on what the present division is based.
I should like to say a word or two with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo. It may be recalled that, when the defence estimates came up last November, he questioned if enough was being spent on the air force; and moved, I think, by nothing but the most serious considerations, he put forward a rather extreme case for that arm of the services. I said we were putting due emphasis on the air force, and were going to do more, that it was in accordance with our plans; and, as he indicated today, that is being done. Today he questions if the navy is getting enough. He asked if the increase in the appropriation for the navy was in any way matching up to the requirements for antisubmarine activities. I should like to give him some figures now which possibly may not be available in the estimates. On a cash basis the estimates and appropriations for the navy are proposed to be increased from $67 million for 1949-50 to $82 million for 1950-51, an increase of 22-4 per cent. That partly reflects the increase in the strength of the navy which is now over its present establishment of 9,047, standing at the 30th of January at 9,322, but mostly the increase in the proposed appropriation for the navy is due to our desire to meet exactly the thing that the hon. member had in mind, the necessity of constructing anti-submarine vessels of a type and character designed, equipped and manned to meet the threat of any submarine that can sail the seas.
Incidentally, I would not accept the hon. member's suggested figures for either the speed or the capacities of submarines so far developed, although that may be a possibility in the not too distant future. We are developing these anti-submarine vessels just because we recognize, and have ever since the end of the war, the need for the kind of thing that the hon. gentleman now mentions. So far as I know, our ships when they are produced will be at least up to and probably in advance of any other anti-submarine vessels. The hon. member also asked about the capacity of frigates, corvettes and destroyers to deal with modern high-speed submarines.
Our position in that respect is the same as any other country's. We do not like the situation that exists today, and we are doing what
14, 1950
Proposed National Defence Committee we can to meet it. We are doing just as much as the Canadian parliament, and the Canadian people, will enable us to do. We believe that our anti-submarine vessels, our destroyers which are undergoing modifications for antisubmarine work, and our other vessels will be able to do the job.
The hon. member also raised some question about the R.C.A.F. interceptors, the number of squadrons and so on. The member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) said our plan to have Vampires was a miserable failure. I hope he is not' serious about that, and I do not think he is. If he is, I do not think he knows the record made by Vampires throughout the world. I do not think he recognizes that these Vampires were the best aircraft we could get for this interim period, and that Vampires, winterized and equipped by us in Canada to meet the conditions of Arctic warfare, behaved magnificently during Exercise Sweetbriar.
Then, what are we doing? We are going on to produce the F-86A, which has the world's record for speed. I think it is by far the most effective single seater interceptor plane in the world. We are also producing the CF-100. Hon. members who, in common with the member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), saw the demonstration of that aircraft last Saturday, will I think agree with me that we have a real aircraft. It is more powerful than any fighter aircraft yet produced. When it is equipped with the Orenda engine, after it has been flight tested, that aircraft will be still more powerful. Hon. members who saw that demonstration of air power no doubt feel that' we are moving along in the right direction. This aircraft is designed to suit Canadian conditions-long range, all weather, navigational instruments, and the capacity to do the kind of job which it was indicated by Exercise Sweetbriar might have to be done if some future eventuality occurs, which we hope will not occur.
The hon. member for Nanaimo and others referred to Exercise Sweetbriar as if it had been in some sense a failure with regard to Canadian forces, aircraft, or equipment employed. I was there. I talked with the officers and men of United States forces and Canadian forces. I heard no such remarks from any of those who were on the spot. I found, as I am sure he would have found had he been there, that we had reason to be proud of the way in which the Canadian staff, the Canadian servicing corps and above all the men of the P.P.C.L.I., the artillery and the other people who were out for eleven days in the exercise but almost seven weeks altogether, withstood the rigours of the north. They came through with magnificent physique, and in high spirits.

Proposed National Defence Committee
As for this charge that they did not have the required aircraft to do the job of airlift, the hon. member must be familiar with some of the facts about airlifts. My recollection, and I am only speaking from recollection, of the time when the Germans came into the low countries is that they had a total of 2,200 airborne troops. My recollection is that when we came back, and made that great air attack on Arnhem, it took the airlift of the United Kingdom, the United States and ourselves working a shuttle service to get in the airborne troops. Now the hon. member knows just as well as I do how many aircraft it takes to lift an airborne brigade; and how many it takes to lift an airborne division in one lift. But that is not the way it is done, because it is not possible for any country in the world to do it that way. I saw the airlift in to the final moment of the exercise at North way. They came in three flights of Dakotas. I must say I never saw anything finer than the sticks of men coming out of the aircraft, their bodies almost horizontal, then swinging down to the perpendicular position, the parachutes opening up and all of them landing almost in a row. It was a superb operation. We had Dakotas then. I do not know of any country in the world that has anything better than Dakotas to do that job, except the United States. Their aircraft for that job are of the C-82 and C-119 types. The United States had two C-82's at Sweet-briar, and we had a good many more Dakotas. They had no C-119's. We have contemplated buying the C-119, and we have even contemplated making it in Canada. At this particular moment, it is felt we just cannot afford it. Each of those aircraft would cost over half a million dollars, and with a year's supply of spare parts as well as the modifications, it might well run into a million dollars.
It is felt that this exercise has shown that the defence of our northwest, which is important beyond words, is an operation in joint . defence. In that operation, the Canadians took just as great a part, and did just as well, as the fine forces of the United States. When you move up the highway from Whitehorse to Snag, and then cross over into Alaska, it takes a cut boundary line to tell where the boundary is. No enemy would ever respect that boundary. The defence of that country must be done as a joint or combined operation. As matters stand, we will play our part, a proper, fair, honest, respectable and respected p rt, in any combined operation.
I am afraid, sir, that I have anticipated something of what I was going to say next Friday and have also delayed the house too long, because I am sure some hon. members are anxious to get into supply and discuss other matters of real importance, in addition

to defence. The hon. member for Middlesex East referred to the Royal Military College at Kingston. I wonder if he has ever been there? I should like to ask him if he has ever been there. I was there following the demonstration of the CF-100 and the transport aircraft, equally good in its field.

On Saturday I motored down and assisted in laying the cornerstone of a new building and then attended a hockey match. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) is quite right. And I was extremely pleased to be present at a hockey game and see R.M.C. win over West Point for the first time since 1938! But I saw, as I have seen on four or five visits I have made to that college over the last year, the work being done, the bearing of the cadets, the quality of the staff, and the amount of research work that is being done by the staff; and I honestly wonder if the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White), whom I respect, should not accept from me an invitation to go there and see what is going on. I think he would come back and say that it was a good thing for Canada that we had a college like that.
In conclusion I should like to refer to some remarks, in that connection and others, of a great general, Field Marshal Earl Wavell, who, in an article appearing in the Sunday Times of December 18, 1949, and headed "A Great Nation's Greater Future", had this to say:
My visit was primarily a military but unofficial one, to the Black Watch of Canada, which most proudly and worthily upholds the traditions and reputation of the oldest Highland regiment. I had also an opportunity at Ottawa and at Kingston, where the staff college and Royal Military College are very pleasantly situated on lake Ontario, of learning something of Canada's military ideas and progress. They seem to me eminently sensible.
Then he went on:
Canada has gone farther on the road to the integration of the three fighting services than any other country. There is a single defence budget; and while I was in Ottawa a bill was passed providing for a common code of discipline for all three services. The Royal Military College at Kingston trains cadets for all three services together: they looked to me a very likely lot of lads. The graduates of the staff college, also a combined one, whom I saw on the last day of their course, were obviously keen and efficient.
Canada does not attempt to maintain a large force in being, but does manage to keep alive the military spirit which proved itself on the battlefields of two great wars; and to be prepared to raise the forces necessary for any fresh emergency without undue delay. In political affairs, too, 1 should say that Canada gets herself governed-
And here perhaps we should hide our blushes.

maintopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is he a qualified observer?

maintopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The article continues:
-with a maximum of quiet efficiency and a minimum of fuss and interference. As a proof of her political stability, it is worth while to note that in the eighty-two years since federation in 1867 Canada has had only 12 prime ministers and 17 ministries.
And then these words:
A great nation already, Canada has a still greater future.
That, Mr. Speaker, is my belief. It is also my belief that the armed forces of Canada are today working to secure that future. From what I have seen of them-and I venture to say that I have seen a great deal more than has any other hon. member in this house-my belief is that they are people with whom it is good to work. They are good citizens first; they are good Canadians; and they are good soldiers.
I must say I am sure that they, like myself and all others concerned with our national defence, welcome every kind of suggestion and every offer of co-operation so that our armed forces can become better still; because Canada deserves nothing but the best.

When the hon. member for Nanaimo gives voice to the views he has expressed here as to the necessity for a committee of this kind, he is doing so out of a background of experience unique in this house; and he is doing so as a man who rose from the ranks to the command of a division. From the experience he has had he knows, better than anyone else, of the high qualities of Canadian troops in every kind of active service. It is out of that experience that he has made this motion that is now before the house.
Tonight we have listened to the Minister of National Defence give the strongest argument that has yet been presented in this house for the committee that is asked for by this motion. It is extraordinary, Mr. Speaker, how sometimes quite innocently a strong argument can be given. The Minister of National Defence just read a statement by a great soldier. Lord Wavell was one of the outstanding officers of the last war. But, like everyone else, Lord Wavell can be misled by propaganda.

I think it would be very interesting for hon. members to read the article and obtain some information as to the problems that are being considered by the department. In this article we find this statement:
Last year we spent $145,033,051 on construction and maintenance of buildings, equipment, food and other supplies through 65,308 contracts placed through our crown-owned purchasing agency.
That is an interesting figure, because it indicates the extent of the interest hon. members should have in this department.
Why is it suggested that there should be an opportunity to examine these accounts in a way that cannot be done here? It is most unfortunate that the Minister of National Defence should so underestimate the intelligence of the people of Canada, if not the

best be spent with economy on the one hand and with efficiency in the actual military preparation on the other.
This subject is not one that has only arisen by way of suggestion that we should try to change our constitutional procedure. On the contrary, here is the mother of parliaments, as the Minister of National Defence has described it, going into their estimates with a committee whose evidence is printed in full and handed to the house. This is only one of the reports that they make each year on this subject. Why the difference between the Minister of National Defence today and the man he was in 1943? Why has all this change come about? In 1943, as has already been stated, and quoted, he then made one of the strongest arguments possible in regard to setting up a committee on national defence- under our system, not the American system. He pointed out that before a committee of the house there could be an inquiry into the army, the navy and the air force, where members of all parties in the House of Commons could sit around and have evidence brought before them and, in an impartial manner, reach conclusions that would be of assistance to the whole house.
Why the change?
Then he was parliamentary assistant, I believe, to the then prime minister; and in that capacity, and with that experience, he thought then there should be a committee on national defence. But now, as Minister of National Defence, he suggests to us that this would be contrary to the constitution and that it would, in fact, be an attempt to accept the American system of government, which is so unlike our own. To use his exact words -"It is an appeal to change our constitutional system, because it is not anything less than that."
Mr. Speaker, within the bounds of parliamentary procedure, it is not possible to use words that describe language of that kind, in relation to what the reality is. And after all, is it not remarkable that it should be so unconstitutional to have a committee on national defence when it is perfectly constitutional to have a committee on external affairs? And yet these are twin departments which are related to the maintenance and security of this country.
The Department of External Affairs is closely related to the Department of National Defence-so closely related, in fact, that the Department of External Affairs must, for instance, screen the arrangements which are made for the export of arms. Naturally that is something in which the Department of National Defence is not interested. But when I hear statements made about the lack of

maintopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to continue this because it has reference to the problem. I quote:
All Mr. Claxton's talk that "it all depends on the time element" and his insistence that these things must be considered in relation to "the likelihood and scale of attack" are so much camouflage. We

Proposed National Defence Committee trust that in. the coming session the Minister of National Defence will not be allowed to dodge this issue any more.
For a start, M.P.'s should insist on being told whether Canada possesses any operational forces, in the strict sense of the word, at all. By "operational forces" we mean combat units which could take the field and engage an enemy immediately. Mr. Claxton makes much of what he calls the "time element"-but it seems to us a very dangerous doctrine to suppose that there would be any time element at all in an emergency.
Then I come to a paper which has not always been unfriendly to the government, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, which states:
Since Mr. Claxton made almost forty-six speeches during his western trip, it must be assumed that he considered his junket, in part at least, as a public relations job. From this point of view his performance in Saskatoon (where he made four speeches) must be judged a failure. Our minister of defence has come and gone and we are no better informed on the principles governing our defence experts' thinking, on the state of our armed forces, on the part we play in the Atlantic association, than we were before he came. In a city keenly aware of the threat from the north Mr. Claxton found himself unable to rise above bromides and platitudes.
And later on:
So far Mr. Claxton and his colleagues have refused to give us anything to work on. It is literally true that the average Canadian knows more about the size, equipment and disposition of the American forces than he does about his own.
He also knows more about the principles upon which American planners base the defence of the continent than he does about what our own planners are thinking. For a few dollars he can buy Vannevar Bush's recent book, "Modern Arms and Free Men", and learn more about the technical developments in warfare and their implications than Canadian officials have released in the past decade.
In case it may be suggested that there is any attempt simply to quote those papers that might not be unduly favourable, let me quote the Toronto Daily Star which has not been regarded as extremely unfavourable to the government. In the closing paragraph of an editorial headed, "Canada's national security", they say:
As defence problems ought to be considered on an all-party basis, it seems not unreasonable that parliament should have a defence committee in which the utmost frankness consistent with safety should prevail. Should occasion arise, the committee could go into secret session to hear confidential reports. The committee, however, should not be given a status that would relieve the defence minister or the government of any of their responsibility for maintaining national security.
That editorial reflects the general opinion that has been expressed across the country in regard to the desirability of bringing these subjects under consideration, finding out exactly what it is we are spending money on, whether in fact we really have a defence force consistent with the needs of Canada at this time, whether more than $600 million is going to be properly spent on this particular occasion, and also, remembering the words

of the minister, whether contracts that run into thousands of dollars are being properly dealt with and properly let.
One could not help of course feeling a great interest in the study group of the Liberal party which unfortunately caused so much misunderstanding, but it was rather interesting that when Mr. Low was giving his explanation it did not embrace quite as wide a field. They were having an informal chat about matters connected with the letting of contracts, and it was doubtless a very informal chat, but at least it is interesting that the method by which these thousands of contracts are let is subject to study, and we hope that study will be extended to the advantage of the people of Canada if not to the others who are concerned.
So far as the amendment is concerned, it is nothing but the most blatant evasion to suggest for one moment that there is any breach of our constitutional practice called for in setting up a committee on national defence. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is asking for a committee.

maintopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: You are opposing it.

maintopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The minister must be a mindreader. I have not spoken on that subject yet. If it is unconstitutional to have a committee dealing with the problems of the Department of National Defence it is equally unconstitutional to have a committee dealing with the problems of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of External Affairs, or any other department of the government. It is the most meaningless evasion that this house has heard. It is simply an attempt to dodge the responsibility of presenting to the house information which every member should have. The minister talks about the information that is given on the estimates, but what earthly opportunity is there for any hon. member to get down to any detail that would help determine whether or not the money is being properly spent? Look at the bulk figures even in what is given in the details of the estimates. You will find there such figures as $22,492,208 for acquisition, construction, purchase, maintenance, repairs, rentals and operating expenses of properties for the army. A fine chance there is for anyone in this house to fulfil his obligation to find out what the money is being spent for or even whether money is being lost. What about the military camp that dis-r appeared at Farnham? What about other military camps that have almost walked away? We have a right and a duty to find out exactly what has happened to that government property. The only place we can do

so is before a committee of this kind. Before hon. members of the house applaud the remarks of the minister in evading his responsibility in this way it would be well for them to bear in mind that we are dealing with the national defence of Canada, and that every one of them knows perfectly well that they will get no information on the discussion of the estimates which will make it possible for them to determine whether or not the money is being properly spent.
Undoubtedly it would take time. Undoubtedly it would involve the attendance of officers before that committee just as it involved staff officers before the committee in Great Britain last year, and as it will involve the attendance of staff officers this year. It took time, but it also presented an opportunity for that house to get the actual information. If the issues are unpleasant to face then they are too dangerous to hide. After all, facts are the very foundation of our democracy, and it is the duty of members of this house to support an amendment which calls for the production of the facts in the one and only way that they can be obtained. In spite of the remarks of the minister and the way in which this has been done, I still hope that he will concur in the amendment when it is presented.
